Modern crotales are arranged chromatically and cover up to two octaves, and the written part is usually two octaves below the sound. In the orchestra, Berlioz's Roméo et Juliette (1839) is one of the early uses, and they later appear in works by Debussy, Ravel and Dutilleux. Today John Adams and Julia Wolfe also use them in orchestral and oratorio works; rock drum kits, musical-theatre line-ups and live shows adopt them too, which shows how they have spread from the orchestra into popular music.

Crotales are small tuned idiophones, struck, Hornbostel–Sachs 111.22. The form is a bronze or brass disc about ten centimetres across, flat on top with a boss underneath, thicker and larger than a tuned finger cymbal, with fine grooves on the surface. They are mostly struck with a hard mallet, and two can also be struck together or bowed; the timbre is like a small tuned bell but brighter and with a longer ring. Modern sets are arranged chromatically and can cover two octaves, and the written part is usually two octaves below the actual pitch. They appear in orchestral, modern and popular rock music, for example Berlioz's Roméo et Juliette and Debussy's Prélude à l'après-midi d'un faune, and rock drummers use them on the kit and in live shows.
